subtopic: CHANGES IN POLICY WITH RESPECT TO OATS AND BARLEY

speakeroldname: Right Hon. J. G. GARDINER (Minister of Agriculture):
subtopic: CHANGES IN POLICY WITH RESPECT TO OATS AND BARLEY
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, it has been suggested by a number of members of the house that as soon as possible a statement should be made with regard to the production of coarse grains in 1947. With your consent, I should like to read that statement to the house now.
83106-90J
The production of dairy products, meat, poultry and eggs in 1947-48 will depend upon the feed supplies available in the form of pasture, fodder, and grain crops.
The pasture, and to a large extent the fodder, acreage for 1947-48 are already determined. Farmers may increase the yields of both of these by the use of fertilizers to the extent that they can be made available, but the weather will be the determining factor in the quantity of feed produced from these sources.
The summer production of beef and dairy products largely depends on pasture, but the quantity of the product can be increased and the quality improved by the use of grain.
The winter production of beef and dairy products will depend upon the supplies of fodder and grain available. The production of pork, poultry and eggs, however, is dependent upon feed grain supplies throughout the year.
Practically all the feed grain supplies produced in 1946-47 have been consumed in the production of meats, dairy products, poultry and eggs. It is therefore not possible to increase the production of meats, dairy products, poultry and eggs in 1947-48 above the quantities produced in 1946-47 unless larger feed grain supplies can be made available.
In order to stimulate production of feed grains and to assure domestic supplies, the government has therefore decided to make a number of changes in policy affecting oats and barley. These changes are as follows:
1.	Effective tomorrow, March 18, the system of advance equalization payments will be discontinued and the Canadian wheat board will stand ready to buy all oats and barley offered to it at new support prices. In the case of barley these prices will be based on 90 cents for No. 1 feed barley, in place of the former support price of 56 cents, in store Fort William/Port Arthur, and other grades at appropriate differentials to be fixed from time to time by the wheat board. In the case of oats, the new support prices will be based on 611 cents for No. 1 feed oats, in place of the former support price of 40 cents, in store Fort William/Port Arthur, and other grades at appropriate differentials to be fixed from time to time by the wheat board. These support prices will remain in effect until July 31, 1948.
2.	At the same time, price ceilings for all grades will be raised, in the case of barley to 93 cents and in the case of oats to 65 cents,
basis in store Fort William/Port Arthur, or
140S
Agricultural Prices

Vancouver. The ceiling prices correspond with the support prices for the highest grades of barley and oats.
3.	In order to avoid discrimination against producers who have already delivered barley during the present crop year, an adjustment payment will be made of 10 cents per bushel in respect of deliveries between August 1, 1946, and March 17, 1947, inclusive, thus raising overall returns to about 90 cents per bushel. As there is a loss in the barley equalization account for the 1946-47 crop year, no further payments are to be expected in respect of barley delivered during the present crop year. The oats equalization account for the crop year 1946-47 will, however, remain open, and net profits in that account, if any, will be distributed later to producers who delivered oats during the period August 1, 1946, to July 31, 1947.
4.	In order to avoid the fortuitous profits to commercial holders of oats and barley that would otherwise result from the action that has been described, handlers and dealers will be required to sell to the wheat board on the basis of existing ceilings of 64} cents for barley and 514 cents for oats, all stocks in their possession at midnight tonight, March 17. Under certain conditions these stocks will be returned to the holder for resale. Allowances will be made for the purpose of taking care >f such items as carrying charges in terminal jositions, special selection premiums, etc., which are considered, in the judgment of the board, fair and reasonable.
5.	For the time being, because of the continuation of price ceilings on animal products, payments of 10 cents per bushel for oats and 25 cents per bushel for barley will be made within the same conditions as the 2S cent payment on wheat purchased for feeding purposes. The payment of these subsidies will have the effect of leaving the cost of these feed grains to feeders approximately at their present levels. I might add that I will shortly ask that a sum be voted to cover the cost of these feed subsidies.
6.	And, finally, the wheat board, either
directly or through agents will become the sole exporter of oats and barley. Any exports by the board will be from grain acquired by the board under the price support plan and the net profits therefrom will be paid into equalization accounts for the benefit of producers.	[DOT]
It is necessary to make a fairly detailed statement of these changes so as to clarify the position of the various interests concerned, but, from the point of view of producers, the important point is that they will now have 
an additional return of approximately 10 to 13 cents per bushel for all the barley they market from this date forward and several cents a bushel on the better grades of oats, over and above the total returns they have been receiving during the present crop year. In addition, producers will continue to receive any net export profits realized by the board as an additional payment at the end of the season.	*
Feeders, on the other nand, will be protected against any important increase in costs of the oats and barley they buy by appropriate subsidies, until the release of the products they sell from ceiling price controls. It will be observed that under this plan buyers and sellers may trade with each other without the intervention of the board, within the limits of the new floors and ceilings.
As I have indicated on previous occasions, it is the policy of the government to continue to pay freight on grain for feeding purposes and mill feeds shipped east from Fort William/ Port Arthur and west from Calgary and Edmonton into British Columbia until July 31, 1948.
As these decisions come into effect, floor prices will be maintained for meats, dairy products and eggs, mainly through the operation of the British contracts. For butter, which is not under contract for shipment to Britain, the dairy products board will be authorized to establish a floor by making purchases during the season of heavy production.
In order to assure supplies to fill the contracts and to make adequate provision for Canadian needs, it is proposed to regulate exports and imports of all products which are subject to contract. This would be done under authority of legislation which is now before the house.
In any case in which a price increase or substitution of a price for a subsidy would have the effect of giving unwarranted profits to holders of stocks, such stocks will be purchased by the government at the old price and returned to the holders or sold at the new price. This procedure will make it possible to recover subsidy or prevent chance profits to the holders of stocks. I want to emphasize this point in order to discourage any hoarding in anticipation of increases in ceiling prices or withdrawal of subsidy that may take place in the future.
The government also wishes to announce that it intends to authorize the wheat board to increase its buying price for flaxseed, effective on August 1, 1947, from the present level

In reply to questions asked by the hon. members for Fraser Valley (Mr. Cruickshank) and New Westminster (Mr. Reid) I wish to state that the floor price on eggs was increased by one cent a dozen for the months of February to August, and by two cents a dozen for the months from September to January, prior to the increase in the cost of feed wheat. In addition, provision has been made for an increase of one-half cent per dozen to cover increased cost of packages, which increase would otherwise have been charged to producers. Furthermore, with the concurrence of the Minister of Finance I am announcing that the wartime prices and trade board will remove the ceiling on shell eggs forthwith.

subtopic: INQUIRY RESPECTING HAINES CUT-OFF

speakeroldname: Hon. BROOKE CLAXTON (Minister of National Defence):
subtopic: INQUIRY RESPECTING HAINES CUT-OFF
speechtext:
Last Thursday the hon. member for Skeena (Mr. Archibald) asked me a question as to a letter said to have been written by General Eisenhower, regarding the closing of the Haines cut-off from the Alaska highway. At that time I thought the hon. member's question was primarily with regard to General Eisenhower's letter and I said that I had not seen this and did not know what it said but that as the road had never been completed it was not going to be closed in the ordinary sense. On.Friday, the hon. member made another inquiry as to what was meant by this.
The Haines cut-off, as it is called, is a road 145 miles long, running from the Alaska highway through sections of the Yukon, the province of British Columbia and Alaska to Haines on an inlet from the sea. The Haines cut-off was under construction by the United States government during the war and it was never completed in that several portions are not gravelled and certain bridges are of temporary construction only. In dry weather in summer time there has been no difficulty in travelling the road with any ordinary vehicle, and as far as the Canadian government is concerned the road has not been closed. Over part of the road the snowfall is heavy and the location of the road makes it very difficult to clear the snow. Steps are not now being taken to complete or maintain the road.

Mr. Speaker, on Friday last the hon. member for Nanaimo (Mr. Pearkes) asked me a question arising out of a statement I had made on Thursday as to the discontinuance of international allocation of fish. I had said that allocation of salted cod and other salted groundfish from Canada's 1946 production would come to an end on June 30 next and that there would be no allocation of such fish from 1947 production. My hon. friend mciuired whether I had reference to all types of salted fish or only to groundfish and, in particular, he wished to know whether restriction on the salting of herring would be removed.
My reference, Mr. Speaker, was to salted groundfish onlj-. As a matter of fact, no other salted fish were ever under international allocation, although, for a time, certain of these other salted products were subject to allocation by our own food requirements committee. This latter control ended on December 31 last. As for herring salting, my hon. friend presumably had in mind dry-salting of herring on the Pacific coast. During the war we halted this dry-salting in certain areas so that a maximum quantity of herring might be available for canning. This restriction ends on March 31.

Mr. ST. LAURENT: Production of the documents requested would require the consent of the governments concerned. Moreover, most of the papers are secret or confidential.
Since the question of preference is most closely related to the subject matter of the united nations trade discussions which began in London last October, the present position on preferences in their relation to the trade discussions can be found in the report of the first session of the preparatory committee of the united nations conference on trade and employment, which I tabled some weeks ago.
I believe it would be quite useless to ask for the consent of the other government, with respect to the tabling of correspondence that has been exchanged as secret and confi-

Motions for Papers
dential. A similar question was raised in the House of Commons at Westminster on January 28, 1947. Mr. Belcher, replying for the president of the Board of Trade, said:
In accordance with the procedure agreed at the meeting of the preparatory committee in London last autumn, the various countries concerned are addressing requests for tariff adjustments to each other as a preliminary to the tariff negotiations which are to be held concurrently with, and as part of the work of, the second session of the preparatory committee later this year. It would be improper to make public the contents of such requests.
As regards the general question of imperial preference, however, I would invite the hon. member's attention to the statement about the Anglo-American financial agreement made by the Prime Minister in the House of Commons on December 6, 1945.
Because of the widespread interest in this matter, perhaps I might be permitted to place on Hansard the statement made by Mr. Attlee in that connection, and which represents what the position still is in that regard. He said:
There is one particular matter arising out of the terms of article VII of the mutual aid agreement which is of especial interest and importance to thq British commonwealth and empire- that is the question of tariff preferences. I would therefore refer shortly to that aspect of the American document which deals with both tariffs and tariff preferences.
The statement sets forth the procedure to be followed by common consent in considering, in the context of a general lowering of tariffs and other trade barriers, what contribution can be made from our side by way of reduction or elimination of preferences.
The statement makes it clear that, in pursuit of the objectives of article VII of the Mutual Aid agreement, we for our part are ready to agree that the existing system of preferences within the British commonwealth and the empire will be contracted, provided there is adequate compensation^ in the form of improvement in trading conditions between commonwealth and empire countries and the rest of the world.
The statement further provides that in entering negotiations for the reduction of tariffs the parties concerned will not refuse to discuss the modification of particular preferences on the ground that these are the subject of prior commitments; on the contrary, all margins of preference will be regarded as open to negotiation, and it will of course be for the party negotiating the modification of any margin of preference which it is bound by an existing commitment to giye a third party, to obtain the consent of the third party concerned.
Further points to be noted are:
(i)	The statement makes it clear there is no commitment on any country in advance of negotiations to reduce or eliminate any particular margin of preference. The position is that each country remains free to judge in the light of the offers made by all the others, the extent of the contribution it can make towards the realization of the agreed objectives.
(ii)	It is recognized that reduction or elimination of preference can only be considered in relation to and in return for reductions of
83166-91*
tariffs and other barriers to world trade in general which would make for mutually advantageous _ arrangements for the expansion of trade. There is thus no question of any unilateral surrender of preferences. There must be adequate compensation for all parties affected.
The statement does not in advance of the detailed negotiations lay down how far the process of reduction and elimination of preferences will be carried at this immediate stage. It must be realized that some preferences are of particular importance to the economy of certain parts of the world just as some tariffs are important in others. The elimination of all prefer* ences would be such a step as would require a most substantial and widespread reduction of tariffs and other trade barriers by a large number of countries. Thus it is recognized that the degree to which the final objectives can be reached at the initial stage can only appear at the negotiations themselves and as the result of a mutually advantageous settlement.
All the subsequent correspondence that has been asked for since has been along the lines of that statement,

On looking over the list of bonuses I find that there is no consistency in the amounts or in the proportions of the increase. In a considerable number of cases the original contract price was more than doubled by the bonus. That is a serious situation, that a person should take a contract under tender and then apply for an increase because of circumstances which existed at the time he got the contract, and that he should receive jn amount in excess of the original contract price. I am not going to refer to all the examples.
As I have been able to work it out, there were fifty cases in which the mail carrier was able to get more than twice the amount he actually bargained for. The list reveals a situation that points to unfairness if not discrimination. While I have the assurance of the mnister that there has been no discrimination, on the other hand there can be no doubt that there has been the greatest unfairness in the award of the bonuses, because of this fact if for no other, that the only ones who got the bonus were those who asked for it, and the only ones who asked for the bonus were those who were aware of its existence.
In Saskatchewan a number of the carriers had no information whatsoever on the fact that a bonus was to be paid. I would ask the minister, in making payment of the bonus, to assure fairness to all the carriers everywhere in Canada. Even today, where there has been unfairness by reason of too large amounts being granted, reconsideration should be given those cases. The information that was put on Hansard the other day was that the post office had made a surplus of some $11 million last year, and the amount was somewhat larger the year before. Mr. Speaker, I should like to speak briefly on this bill before it is given third reading. I have examined the report tabled by the Postmaster General (Mr. Bertrand) setting out bonuses paid to rural mail drivers, as authorized by order in council. It reveals that many rural mail carriers received bonuses much larger than their original contracts, while others received no bonuses at all. Here are some examples of bonuses being paid in amounts greater than the original tenders. In the first of these the original contract was for $308 and the bonus paid was $592. In the second instance the contract price was $360 and
the bonus $480. Another shows a contract price of $302 with a bonus of $339, and still another gives a contract price of $308 with a bonus of $365.
We may compare these figures with others, one of which gives a contract price of $500 and a bonus of only $85. I cannot see where there is any comparison at all. This report reveals that on a mileage basis some drivers receive as much as $77 while others receive only $20.
I am sure all hon. members will agree that mail drivers should receive remuneration sufficient to enable them to carry out their duties efficiently, and also that there should be a system of equitable remuneration for services rendered. In my own riding I find that out of some fifty contracts, twenty-four received no bonuses whatever, and apparently these men had no idea that bonuses were being paid. Under the present hocus-pocus-or-bonus-bonus-who-will-get-the-bonus system, the whole thing is nothing less than a farce and should be changed as soon as possible. I do not think these men can be equitably paid under the present system. A mileage basis of payment would not be equitable when one driver's route is over rough country or township roads, up and down hill, and another driver's route is over paved roads. Nor do I think mail drivers should be paid on the basis of the number of boxes on their routes.
May I be allowed to make a suggestion which I think would improve the system of rural mail delivery. I would suggest that all mail drivers be paid on an hourly basis. A survey could be made to determine the actual time it takes for a driver to cover his route, having regard only to the delivery of His Majesty's royal mail and other duties pertaining thereto. Allowance should be made also for the use of horses in extremely bad w'eather. Having arrived at the number of hours it takes to cover a certain mail route, I suggest that the driver be paid at the rate of $1.10 or SI .20 per hour. That rate would cover the driver's time and the use of his car or horses or other type of vehicle. I think this would give the driver a reasonable amount for gasoline and oil and depreciation on his equipment.
A mail route requiring five hours to cover would work out to $5.50 per day, with the yearly remuneration on the basis of 312 days amounting to $1,710. I think that would be a fair basis on which to pay rural mail drivers. This system would permit the driver to purchase good equipment of a uniform nature, as I mentioned the last time I spoke on this matter. I suggested that the equipment possibly could be a standard coach,
Postal Service

with all cars painted a similar colour. Then there could be attached a sign bearing the coat of arms and reading, "His Majesty's Royal Mail." This sign would not be allowed on the car when it was not being used for the delivery of His Majesty's mail. A driver might need his car for only three or four hours a day and would want to make use of it at other times for other purposes, so the sign would be permitted on the car only when it was being used for the delivery of the mail. Last time I suggested that these cars might be painted red, but after considering that they would be driven over dusty roads, and having been in the car business for a number of years, I would now suggest grey or gunmetal, with a red sign to be put on or taken off.
I offer these suggestions realizing that while they may not be perfect they might offer a means of improving one of our services which is of paramount importance to our country, and of bringing about a better distribution of His Majesty's mail.

Mr, Speaker, I thank those who have taken part in this debate. Some ideas have been expressed which in the beginning appeared to be good, but which, when examined, did not measure up so well. We must begin at the beginning; we must remember we are dealing with people who have tendered, who have asked for a contract at a certain price. It may be absolutely true to say this is unfair to some who did not ask for enough, but if we indict the tender system today in regard to rural mail delivery or any other mail contracts, we indict the tender system generally; and heretofore it has been recognized by all parties that the tender system for contracts is the fairest system we have been able to find.
Of course we could follow another system and pay a contractor so much an hour, after naving found out for ourselves how many hours it would take to fulfil a contract, on good and bad days. When this question was first argued, however, quite a number of hon. members on the other side said that we had in our hands what they called a pork barrel, that asking permission to make supplementary payments to certain people constituted a pork barrel of the first magnitude. Well, if we were to give contracts to gentlemen at so much an hour, and, in addition, pay for the gasoline used and so on, we would no longer have any people to tender, and we would have

Postal Service
a real pork barrel in our hands which would oermit us to give these contracts to whomever we wished.
This is the point we had in mind at the headquarters of the Post Office Department for many years when we were considering what we should do in order to help these rural mail contractors. Perhaps I might tell hon. members a very short story. Once I was appearing for the respondent in a case before the court of appeal in Montreal. M3' adversary was rising and arguing, not exactly following the etiquette which does not permit a lawyer to get up more than once, and I was getting up each time myself to reply; but I was told by Chief Justice Greenshields, who was presiding, that is was not necessary for me to see that my adversary understood the case in order to win it.
I explained most of these matters when this legislation was brought in two weeks ago, but perhaps I should repeat, certain things I said then. Starting with the point that these contracts result from tenders, and that unfortunately there are people who have put in these tenders at prices which are too low; I admit that; otherwise we would not have given any bonuses. Starting with that point, however, I believe it- might well be that someone put in a tender at a price so low that, if something had not been done, he would have had to abandon his contract. In fact many of these people told us they would have to abandon .their contracts unless we gave them a bonus. That was wh>r we passed the second order in council in 1943, which allowed us to make up the discrepancy.
When we adjusted these contracts with those who asked that this be done, we took into consideration certain factors, among many others, because there were factors that had to be taken into consideration, which pertained onlv- to certain types of contracts. We looked at the rate paid for similar services in the same locality. We scrutinized those prices. Special attention was paid to the rates being obtained by tender for other similar services, as indicating a trend. We took note of the date at which the contract was entered into, in order to determine the degree of change in operating costs. If a contract had been granted perhaps only three or four months before the tenderer applied for a bonus, he would not get it, because he must have known at that time that the cost of living was increasing, the cost of labour was going up. The tenderer must have known that material was becoming harder to get, and so on. This will explain why, under the law today, we
cannot grant a bonus to anyone who has had a contract for less than twelve months. If the date at which the contract was entered into was not available, tender results in other areas were accepted as indicating a general trend. Consideration was given .to the general increase in the wages of labour. In certain places that increase was much greater than in others. In Vancouver, for example, we found that the cost of labour had increased much more than in certain cities in the east.

In certain instances we have asked for new tenders. I have given the figures before. Wherever we asked for tenders, the Post Office Department has had to pay more than when we passed on a contract with the same contractor, and granted him a bonus, often the bonus he was asking for. I believe this was better, because a man might have an automobile, or he might have been using horses. It would be better to continue the contract with him and to give him the bonus

than to take a new tenderer at a much higher price than was asked by the one who would continue with the contract price plus bonus.
All applications for bonuses were not granted. There are many cases where the rate asked for is excessive for the work performed, even under existing circumstances. This is a fact which is borne in mind when any proposal to cure the situation by granting a flat increase to all mail contractors is put forward.
Someone referred to the hon. member for Labelle (Mr. Lalonde) and to the fact that in his constituency a large number of mail contractors have had bonuses. Well, in this respect some of the bonuses asked for were abusive, and we then asked for tenders. Some of the tenders came with such high prices that we refused to accept them. The result is that there are two or three rural routes today in the hon. member's constituency where there is no service. We are waiting till such time as we can supply a service at a reasonable price.
In dealing with any application for bonus, steps are taken to ascertain when public tenders were last invited for the service under consideration. If tenders were received within twelve months of the application, the tenders are scrutinized to determine the degree of competition and particularly the rate of the second lowest tender. This is taken into account when deciding the amount of any bonus granted.
We were asked for details, and as a result we prepared these documents which were tabled last week. They were prepared following the request of the hon. member for Lake Centre, and were shown to him before they were deposited in the house. We asked him if he was satisfied with them and he said he was. We have not given the reason why certain figures have been given in each instance, but that information can be obtained by considering the context, and by taking note of the frequency, the number of miles, and the boxes to be served, et cetera.

A number of questions were asked, but most of those questions did not take into account the fact that we are dealing with contracts which were obtained on tender. The basic price was fixed by the contractor who would know the route and who, it would be supposed, would take great care to tender sufficiently to be able to make money. I am quite sure that if that were done a large number of tenderers would bid the minimum price, and then we would have to choose. Mr. Speaker, when the debate was adjourned on Friday night one of the principal speakers on the amendment offered by the hon. member for Mackenzie (Mr. Nicholson) was the Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Gardiner), who gave an interesting talk, informative at times, a bit fantastic in one or two spots, a mixture of fact and fancy of the kind in which the minister frequently indulges.
I do not think there is any doubt in the minds of the members of this particular group about the bill that has been presented doing the job which the minister says the government wants done. We have no doubt about that whatsoever. But we want a lot more. We agree that the contracts which the government have made with other countries must be carried out, and if thiis vehicle is the only one they can conceive of for doing that job, we are not going to stop them from having this vehicle. But we want to make it clear that to us it is simply a horse and buggy compared with what the farmers of this country want. They want the orderly marketing of farm products and cooperative and democratic control of the machinery of that marketing, and we support their demands and will continue to do so on every occasion in this house. We also believe that, while it may be difficult at this late date, a marketing act such as is forecast in the amendment offered by the hon. member for Mackenzie would give the minister and the government an opportunity to do all that can be done under this bill, and, as well, something more. Had it been started early enough and conceived with some of the vision that the Liberal party claims to have, we have not the slightest doubt in our minds that something of that kind could have been done. I think I am safe in saying that

the minister himself believes that, because at the last minute he brought in an amendment to a section of the bill dealing with apples, which indicates that he considers it necessary to have some marketing control over interprovincial trade. That is a clear indication that the minister felt that way from the start.
Another thing we do not like about this bill is that we recognize that these contracts will not last forever. Very few of them expire this year, and this bill terminates at the end of this year. As a matter of fact it is only a nine-months bill, and it will terminate at a time when parliament is not sitting. If there is no election this year-I do not know whether there will be or not; I do not know whether the minister knows-

The bill does imply the possibility of a session of parliament in November and December, which may or may not happen. The bill itself will expire on December 31 next. Some of the contracts, the minister says, will not expire until 1948 and some in 1949. At least contracts for two very large items will not expire until 1949. This means that parliament will have to go through this process year after year until the government finally get rid of these contracts and do something else which they may envisage at that time, if they are still in their seats over there.
The hon. member for Humboldt (Mr. Burton) asked the minister what a transitional period was. The minister was pointing out the transitional nature of this bill. He replied that he did not know what the transitional period would be, and he does not believe that anybody else knows. I agree with the minister that he does not know and that nobody else in this house knows what the transitional period will be. Not even the minister himself can give us a definition of the transition from war to peace or from this period to that, and tell us what wall take place. It is a frank admission that private monopoly enterprise is always in a transitional stage, and we shall always be having bills of this kind unless we frankly face the transitional nature of our present-day society and make plans with some degree of permanence and vision.
There are times when the Liberals believe that they do know when the transitional period will end. They say they believe they know and they have paid out monev at

It has been designed with the aid of the keenest minds in every phase of industry, agriculture, labour and learning.
Some of the keenest minds in agriculture have circulated among the members of this house this document. It is called:
Here is exact demand of Canadian farmers; their draft act for dominion natural products marketing legislation as submitted to cabinet.
That is from the Canadian Federation of Agriculture. I turn back to the advertisement. It says:
The Liberals have a working plan ... It has been designed with the aid of the keenest minds in every phase of industry, agriculture, labour and learning.
I have heard other members deal with the plans of these keen minds regarding labour, education and so forth, and I submit that if this bill has been drawn up with the aid of the keenest minds in agriculture it is a distinct slap in the face for the officials of the Canadian Federation of Agriculture, who believe they have keen minds too. The advertisement goes on to say:
The plan will work. In fact it is already bringing results.
It will continue to do so! The Liberals can tell you this with confidence because they have had successful experience in operating nationwide plans.
I would say that they have had experience in operating on a transitional basis. Some of their operations on a transitional basis would make one smile a little if it were not so annoying.
Just by way of a little interlude, Mr. Speaker, I would exhibit to the house a little sample of private enterprise and planning to indicate some of the things they do during the transitional period. These are Kleenex tissues I hold in my hand. Here is one. This is what private enterprise is making at the present time and, in spite of the demand for the other kind that I have here, almost three times as large, they are supplying this smaller tissue. I ou go into a drugstore to buy the big kind and they offer you the small. I ask, "Why can't I get the larger kind that I want?" The answer is, "They are all sold." The minister took occasion the other day to indulge in quite a bit of fantasy, as he does every once in a while, and one of the most fantastic portions of his speech was his recitation of the experience he had when visiting a certain gentleman who had previously visited Regina. This person had told him about his visit there, and how this visitor had come to the conclusion, from his interviews with government officials there, that the province of Saskatchewan had built up its socialist regime and all its cooperative institutions in the period of a couple of years. Of course the visitor had not known that. The minister implied that he put him right. I think the minister must have been intending to imply some criticism of the C.C.F. which was not fair, and he frequently takes occasion to point out that the Liberal party, particularly in Saskatchewan, is to be credited with the great development of cooperative enterprise in that province. I pay the minister the personal tribute of believing that he is just as proud as I am of the things that have been done in that province in that field. I will admit that the rise of these associations and organizations took place for the most part when the Liberals were in power, but some of them took place when Tory governments were in power. I shall have to refute emphatically, his claim to credit for his party or the claim of any political party.
Let me give a reason for that assertion. The first wheat board was established under a Union government which was neither Liberal nor Tory. The establishment of that board and its operations gave the farmers of the west the idea that there was something good in the principle of orderly marketing. They made a demand for its continuance in 1921 and 1922. At that time we had a Liberal prime minister in Ottawa, a Liberal premier in Saskatchewan and Manitoba and a U.F.A. premier in Alberta. The cooperative wheat producers, that is, the wheat pools, of these provinces arose by the action of the farmers themselves after the failure of the parties I have cited, who had failed to meet the demand which the farmers had made. These organizations were born in spite of the Liberal party and not because of it, and I wish to make that abundantly clear.

When I was first premier of Saskatchewan, between 1926 and 1929, I had all the creameries in Saskatchewan amalgamated under that organization prior to 1929.

Mr. SOLON E. LOW (Peace River): Mr. Speaker, I shall delay the house but a very few minutes in placing before hon. members the position which this group takes with respect to Bill No. 25. The government has made certain international agreements for Canada to supply wheat, bacon, cheese and some other products to other countries. We realize that the government must be able to get the commodities with which to fulfil its commitments under those agreements. The purpose of Bill No. 25 is to provide the machinery by which the government may be able to get those products to fulfil international agreements. We feel that the bill confers on the minister very wide powers which ordinarily we should not like to confer on any minister of the crown. The provisions of the bill are to have effect for only one year; and because it is an emergency transitional bill to meet a certain set of circumstances that have arisen out of war time, this group will not put up a battle on the principle of the bill itself.
We are, however, strongly opposed to giving the minister the right to set up commodity boards as provided for in this bill and clothing them with extraordinary powers which are enunciated in the various clauses thereof. In this respect I would say we are thoroughly in accord with what was said by the hon. member for Yale (Mr. Stirling). We urge the minister to make use of existing producer boards or those which might come into existence later under the various provincial marketing acts. These producer boards, I feel sure, are prepared to cooperate with the federal government in any way that they can. It seems to me that the whole principle of orderly marketing ought to be based upon the fundamental principle of keeping control of the producers' product as close to the producer as possible. Whenever the minister does require certain natural products for the purposes of fulfilling his agreements with Britain or anj- other country, he should direct that such commodities be purchased from the producer boards wherever possible. The obligation for him to do this should be clearly stated in the bill. The measure we are considering does make it possible for the minister to direct the purchase of commodities for the purposes of the act from provincial marketing boards; but, as I read it, there is absolutely no obligation upon him to do so.
I should now like to say just a word in regard to a natural products marketing act.

This group think the government should bring in at a very early day; in fact, we think before this they should have prepared and brought into this house, a bill providing for the orderly marketing of natural products in Canada. I am inclined to agree with the minister that we should not attempt to tack on to this bill, which is for an emergency transitional period, a long-range, comprehensive marketing measure. I do not think it wise to attempt to do that. We consider that the new legislation which should be brought in, and which we are urging the minister in the strongest possible terms to bring in, should be substantially as asked for by the Canadian Federation of Agriculture. Amongst other things it should provide for these: first, for orderly interprovincial and international trading in natural products; second, for the recognition of provincial marketing boards and producer boards as sources of supply. Every encouragement should be given the provinces to put through enabling legislation, under which every effort should be made to organize producer boards, to keep some control over the produce of the farmers right where it belongs, in the hands of the producers themselves. I do not believe it is wise to let these boards rest, in their control of the products raised, on a mere majority. I should say that when a substantial majority, let us say something between seventy and eighty per cent, of the producers of any natural product voluntarily agree to set up a board for control purposes, then I believe the control of the entire supply of that product should be vested in the board. Anything less than seventy to eighty per cent I do not believe could possibly be successful.
The third thing I believe should be in any marketing bill is protection of the right of the producer to be consulted through the medium of his board, particularly by the minister, as to prices and other matters, before he makes agreements with any country which might affect or set the price of the farmer's products. We have seen so many examples in this country of agreements having been made without consulting the producers of the products. Then this parliament has been asked to ratify those agreements, or to take action which would support the minister in fulfilling their terms. Finally, the new marketing legislation should give full recognition to provincial authority over property and civil rights, as is provided in the constitution. The place of the dominion in any long-range marketing scheme should be mainly that of an agent or clearing house for the producer boards and/or the provincial marketing boards.

I wish to refer now to another commodity which I think should be left to the hands of the government to sell and export. I refer to the bean industry. In the part of Ontario from which I come the best cash crop we have is beans, the white pea bean. This government has been negotiating contracts with Great Britain for a few years now for the sale of these beans. Last year it negotiated a contract for 560,000 bushels; and an agreement was made with the farmers through the medium of a bean board, a producer board set up among the farmers in the counties of western Ontario, whereby a certain price would be paid for the beans. The dealers agreed to it. For cleaning, processing and making shipment they got a certain price. The farmers were satisfied and we thought the dealers also were satisfied. The farmers sold beans last fall, but the dealers thought the arrangement was not good enough, that they could make more money out of this farm commodity than they were making.
What has happened? We were asked to ship to Great Britain 560,000 bushels. We had 1,200,000 bushels in that part of Ontario, not a big crop but a good crop. We have sent only 150,000 bushels to Great Britain. Now Britain is asking again for another contract in connection with this commodity, but the dealers are not willing to sell at a price Great Britain can pay. The farmers-and I do not blame them-can see a good price from the 1947 crop looming up. As I say, we do not blame them, but at the same time they are reasonable men and they know that there is no use in getting a big price this fall and a low price next fall. I feel that the bean men of our district should endeavour to help themselves, and I refer to the producers. They should establish a central marketing agency to which these beans could be brought for shipment to Great Britain at a price that Great Britain is willing to negotiate upon. I would ask the government if it would not be
possible for them to negotiate a contract with Great Britain for a five-year period for white beans, just as has been done for wheat, the farmers to bind themselves under a central marketing agency to fill the contract. A down payment could be made and if beans sold, after the contract was filled, at a higher price in the domestic market, a participation certificate would be paid in respect of the balance.
I think I speak for the bean industry of western Ontario when I say that we have a product on which we think we should receive a good return for the labour that we have devoted to it over a period of years. We have this market in Great Britain if only we will help ourselves, and I think the government would cooperate with us in the sale of the commodity and not leave it to the dealers.
I do not wish to discuss this bill any further. As I said, I am wholeheartedly behind it because I feel it is a step in the right direction. The government has been asked by the house to establish floor-price legislation, but how on earth are you going to have floor-price legislation unless you have government support for it? The farmers, from one end of the country to the other, are asking, "When will floor prices come into effect?" I say to the house, as I have said to my own people, that the best floor-price legislation you can have is good markets for your products. WThy should the state not handle this? After all, they are only the representatives of the country. We are a democratic country and, if we are not satisfied with the government that is in power, we have our redress at the next election because we can turn them out.
We heard on Friday and we have heard again today about the national federal marketing legislation which the Canadian Federation of Agriculture are proposing. I am not going to say that I will oppose it when it is brought in, but I do say that we shall look into it thoroughly, because the farmers will expect us to do so. They will expect us to inquire whether it is a good thing for them or not.
In conclusion, I challenge the opposition to vote against this bill, which, I submit, is in the interests of the farmers. I am wholeheartedly behind it.

Mr. Speaker, on Friday last I had a speech on this bill ready for delivery, but I missed my turn and, since then, everybody else has said what I was going to say. I do not intend to impose that speech upon the house tonight, but I will sum up the remarks I intended to make.
I thought the minister, in rising to speak on this bill, would have been able to give the house some assurance that he would bring in something in the nature of a dominion natural products marketing act. I am disappointed about that. When he did not take that action I hoped he would be able to improve this legislation to cover some of the things that would have been of advantage to organized agriculture now. In summing up the situation, the minister had this to say, as reported at page 1394 of Hansard:
Therefore I object to any attempt being made by the house now to put into this act terms which never were intended to be in legislation of this kind; terms which, if they are to be

Agricultural Products Act
enacted at all, ought to be enacted under separate legislation brought into the house, discussed on its merits, and if this is the proper time to pass it, if it must be passed, then it should be passed. But if it is not the proper time to consider it, in view of the fact that organizations are not yet prepared to do the job that is required to be done, then it could be brought in at some other time by whatever government is then in power.
Then he went on to make some comments about the meeting with the Canadian Federation of Agriculture, saying that they had expected that legislation and that he had assured them it could not be introduced this session. I want to tell the minister I am glad further consideration has been given to the apple growers, as he has announced. By this concession the minister admits that the bill is not all that is desired, or all that it should be. He has turned down the request of the Canadian Federation of Agriculture for a dominion natural products marketing act, but I want to remind him that the farm organizations are growing stronger. He should pay heed to the fact that a nation which plans for war knows that, if it did not plan, it would lose the war; but when you suggest planning in peace time in order that maximum production at guaranteed prices may be maintained, this is at once condemned as compulsion. The new idea in marketing, which proved itself in war time, will surely live, though there may be those who will try to strangle it. The farmers have had a good taste of the security and stability that come from guaranteed prices for guaranteed quantities, and the taste has been good. In the last few days a great deal has been said about compulsion. I am going to leave wheat and coarse grains alone for the moment and refer to a pamphlet entitled, "What Ontario fruit and vegetable growers want done in the legislative field." The secretary of the two associations had this to say:
The history of all progress is one of persistent effort especially when dealing with governments. Eternal prodding is the secret of success. Progress is slow.
Signs are not wanting that governments are much concerned these days with the welfare of agriculture. This indicates response to the urgings for it is realized that agriculture cannot, once again, become a mere form of subsistence-That it must be nourished and sustained. Politicians (and, after all. the responsibility is theirs) who fail to take the forward steps will have no reason to be disturbed if others take their place. Systems are on trial. .
The policy makers must show courage and render leadership-political considerations should not prevail nor should powerful groups be permitted to dictate policy because they fear loss of vested privileges.
Most of the opposition to many of agriculture's proposals has come from groups and individuals who, fearful of the unknown, have let prejudice and ignorance sway their judgment.
Farm leaders have developed a sense of responsibility. They are not out to wreck the system nor do they plan harm to others. They are seized with an honest desire to improve the lot of their fellow men but not on a basis of robbing Peter to pay Paul.
Live and let live is the keynote. If legislative action is necessary to establish authority and power to make the principle apply, legislation we must have. Farm organizations dislike running to government for cash aid-they much prefer the authority to do things for themselves.
There must be a certain amount of compulsion if we are to make this system work and have orderly marketing. They do not say, "You cannot grot? fruit or vegetables"; they do not try to deprive any grower of his living. They only want the cooperation of the growers to abide by the decision of the majority so that all may benefit by the united effort. Other organizations go much farther than this, and it is quite all right. The trade unionist working in the union shop expects and insists that his fellow be a trade unionist as well. Even the bar association, or the lawyers' union, makes it compulsory for every lawyer to belong. They will even have a man convicted for trying to do the work of a lawyer without having been admitted to the bar. In support of that statement, I would refer to a clipping from the Winnipeg Free Press of March 6:
Charged with ten breaches of the law society act,-pleaded guilty before Magistrate D. G. Potter in provincial police court Wednesday. He was given a two-year suspended sentence, bound over in the sum of $500 and ordered to pay court costs.
Acting for the law society of Manitoba. A. E. Johnston told the court that this gentleman, notary public and insurance agent, had been drawing up legal documents, closing real estate transactions and acting as solicitor without the proper authority. He said this gentleman had not been called to the bar, and his duties as notary public did not empower him to carry out these acts.

The farm organizations have never gone so far as to stop anyone from being a farmer. Any Tom, Dick or Harry can come along, get a piece of land and produce the necessities of life. The farm organizations have no objection. All they want them to do is to be good fellows and support the organization.
In closing. I wish again to remind the minister that the farmer is demanding legislation that will enable him to run his own business in order that he can get a fair share
Agricultural Products Act

of the consumer's dollar by orderly marketing in both home and export markets; and I would suggest that the minister promise to bring in a bill similar to the one requested by the Canadian Federation of Agriculture at their recent meeting with the cabinet, to bridge the gap between the provinces and the dominion.
Might I say to the minister that I was the seconder of the amendment. You have it in your hands.

speechtext: I never have done any bribing since I have been in politics.

speechtext:
And you can call it black-leg or bootleg, or anything you like. I was sent here by the farmers to get these things. All I am asking you is to give us your word that you will take that up early in the next session. We asked for it in 1939 and you said that the time was not right. We agreed with you. You have been minister all that time, and we have not come back until a time of peace. We are asking you now, in all sincerity, to give us these things. Do not fail us now. I will be prepared to withdraw the amendment. I am going to support your bill, because it is a step in the right direction. I am now awaiting your answer.
As a headline in one of the evening papers I saw a boy delivering on Friday night were the words "British M.P. attacks Canadian wheat prices." On reading the paper, I found that a gentleman by the name of Smithers had made that statement. I am going to quote from the Ottawa Journal of March 14, 1947. Might I say also that he is a Conservative? Wait until you hear what he has to say. Sir Waldron Smithers declared that-
-having been to Canada many times, he knew that "dollar wheat" Showed a good profit.
And then under the heading "Charge against Canadians" we find this:
When Straehey went to Canada recently, he said, the Canadian farmers said: "Here comes this little chap from Britain. His people are very hungry. What is the most we can get out of him?"
To hon. members in this house I say this, that no greater insult could be directed at the farmers of Canada. No greater insult could ever have been heaped upon us. Does this member of the British House of Parliament know what he is talking about? He has a "sir" to his name and no doubt he should know better than make such ridiculous statements as these

attributed to him. Does he know they are getting wheat at $1.55 a bushel? Does he know that the Progressive Conservative party in this parliament have maintained here in the House of Commons that Britain should not have got wheat so cheaply, but should be paying the world price? That, I think, is $2.79 today, if we use the Chicago price.

I hope he reads this, then. Quoting further from the press, we find this:
Sir Waldron urged that food buying be left to purchasing firms with long experience and that healthy competition be permitted.

Upon looking up the "Parliamentary Guide" I find that Sir Waldron is a member of the London stock exchange. Here is a man who has no doubt spent the best part of his life chasing hounds and shooting grouse, a man who has lived by the sweat and toil of others, and who is now calling for the "good old days" which orderly marketing and guaranteed prices will destroy. It makes my blood boil to read this, after what Canada has done to provide food for Britain. But let us hope he is only one in a million.
Here is a letter I received from a lady in Glasgow on Friday last; and I have received many such letters. She says in part:
Many thanks to Canada for our Sunday breakfast. The last three Sundays we have been able to have one strip of bacon and one Canadian egg, which was enjoyed greatly by all of us.
When you go to the people who suffered you find that they do appreciate what Canada did for them. They do not think we are holding them up. I feel I know what I am talking about, because I was over there. Hon. members who were also there will agree with me that Canada has done and is doing everything a sister nation of the British commonwealth could be expected to do. She stood by Britain at Dunkirk; she gave her best sons, who now lie in graves across the sea; she gave her food and munitions, and did everything in her power to support Britain in her time of need.
Having lived for thirty years in the old land, I know this type of gentleman only too well. Most of them have a valet to dress them in the morning. But I am pleased to notice that this type of gentleman is now becoming scarce in the British parliament; most of the members there today can at least put on their own pants.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the hon. member for Selkirk (Mr. Bryce) has been talking about a man named Smithers, and apparently received a

Agricultural Products Act
considerable amount of applause because of that reference. As he was speaking of this chap Smithers, I thought to myself, from his description, how remarkably like Smithers is the Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Gardiner), except, of course, for his stock-broking and grouse shooting activities.

subtopic: PROVISION FOR PURCHASE, SALE AND EXPORT-COMMODITY AND PROVINCIAL MARKETING BOARDS
speechtext: There are other things, too.

subtopic: PROVISION FOR PURCHASE, SALE AND EXPORT-COMMODITY AND PROVINCIAL MARKETING BOARDS
speechtext:
So far as his attitude with respect to wheat is concerned, I think Sir Waldron Smithers is very much the same as our Minister of Agriculture. He is just a little behind; he thinks a dollar a bushel for wheat is all that the western farmer should have, while our Minister of Agriculture, a little more advanced, says it should be 11.35. That is all he is going to pay in the next four years. There is a hope there may be a little left in the kitty after that to supplement it.
However, what I rose particularly to say was this: The hon. member for Fort William (Mr. Mclvor) said that there were two things in this bill which stood out as far as he was concerned. There is only one thing which stands out as far as I am concerned, and it is this: The essential principle of this bill is that the marketing of all agricultural products except wheat, which has already been looked after, is brought completely under the control of the Minister of Agriculture. In other words, this bill makes the Minister of Agriculture practically a dictator as far as the marketing of agricultural products is concerned. That is really why I object to it. I believe the bill as it stands is practically pure and simple socialism and, as a result, I am going to vote against it. As a matter of fact the best feature about the bill is that it has a one-year termination clause. That is about the only good thing I have to say about it.
The bill enables the minister to make new contracts, which I think is one of its most objectionable features. I would be prepared to give the minister all the powers necessary to enable him to meet the contracts which he has made with Great Britain for cheese and bacon and other products. I have no doubt a considerable number of the powers he has asked for in this bill are required for that purpose. However I object most strongly to giving him the power to make new contracts, thereby perpetuating the situation we have at the present time, where the minister brings in a wheat bill and says, "I must have these powers so that we can fulfil our commitments to Great Britain"; or where he brings in this bill and says, "I must have these powers so
that we can fulfil the commitments we have made to Great Britain in the matter of dairy products and so forth."
Is this thing ever going to end or will it continue indefinitely? If the minister has the power to make new contracts a year from now we shall be faced with the situation where he can come back and say, "Here are these contracts which must be met because Canada cannot go back on her word. I must have these powers." Therefore we shall never get away from this socialistic type of legislation which puts into the hands of the minister and the government complete control of the marketing of agricultural products.
I think the hon. member for New Westminster (Mr. Reid) stated an obvious truth when he said that we all realized that times have changed, that we can never go back to the situation which existed ten or fifteen years ago. I think everybody realizes that. I think we realize that, as long as we have to deal with totalitarian countries and countries which engage in state trading, we shall probably have to carry on a certain amount of state trading ourselves. But surely if we are a free enterprise country and are going to continue to be, our efforts should be directed toward getting away from state trading as rapidly as we can and getting things back to the place where we have a free exchange of goods and more or less of a free world market if this can possibly be done. Possibly it is too late and it may never be done, but for goodness sake, let us work toward that goal instead of working in the opposite direction, which I submit this bill does.
I was interested in some of the remarks of the hon. member for Middlesex West (Mr. McCubbin). He asked a question which I laughed over a little. He asked, "Why do I support this bill?" I think it was obvious to everyone in the house why he supported it. He supported it because the Minister of Agriculture introduced it. That was sufficient reason for him. When the Minister of Agriculture introduced the resolution a week or two ago, and when the hon. member for Middlesex West spoke in connection with beef, both said that there was no doubt in the world that the United States was the best market we could have for our beef, that it was our natural market. But both of them immediately turned around and said, "By no means let us send any beef there; it is our best market, but under no circumstances let us send any beef there; let us get as far away from it as we can." Both said, "No, we will not send even a token shipment of beef; it is not necessary; it is not required."

I should like to repeat what I said when the matter was first introduced. I said that a considerable number of the largest beef producers in this country think it is necessary. I said that I thought their advice on the matter should have been listened to by the government, and listened to carefully. I have a great deal more confidence in their judgment on the matter than I have in the judgment of the hon. member for Middlesex West.

speechtext: Mr. Speaker, if I am permitted to say a word about Bill No. 25 it would be this: I am one of those who has waited patiently for a federal agricultural marketing act. At last we have it, but what an act!

subtopic: PROVISION FOR PURCHASE, SALE AND EXPORT-COMMODITY AND PROVINCIAL MARKETING BOARDS
speechtext: You have not it yet.

subtopic: PROVISION FOR PURCHASE, SALE AND EXPORT-COMMODITY AND PROVINCIAL MARKETING BOARDS
speechtext:
That is what I am afraid of. I have listened patiently to a great deal of talk about wheat and I do not propose to mention that commodity, or the fact that our Ontario soft winter wheat has been priced away out of line. I have been intensely interested in the problems that face the primary producer in connection with orderly marketing. I have the privilege of representing a county in southwestern Ontario. Unfortunately for me I was paired with the hon. member for Essex South (Mr. Clark) when the amendment of the hon. member for Yale (Mr. Stirling) was voted upon. I strongly endorsed that amendment. The reason I paired with the hon. member for Essex South was that he is one of those who is most conversant with the marketing problems of our district. I also listened with tremendous tolerance to my very good friend the hon. member for Middlesex West (Mr. McCubbin) when he addressed the house tonight. I immediately went across the floor and congratulated him, and also corrected him on a few mistakes which, in my opinion, he had made.
When the Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Gardiner) brought down this bill I do not know exactly what he had in mind, but I do know from whence the idea came. It came from the producer boards of British Columbia and southwestern Ontario. It was not the child of his own mind at all. He may have been part and parcel, one of those who were in on the play when the Natural Products Marketing Act was booted off the field of Canada's trade. Now he has seen fit to bring it back in a camouflaged form whereby all the power is vested in the minister, giving him absolute control in the marketing of the products that have been brought to his attention. As one of the farmers of this country and having been intensely interested in orderly marketing of the specialized commodities raised in our district, I felt I would be remiss in my duty if I did not bring a few matters to the attention of the minister at this time. I have hesitated all during the war to make myself heard or to be critical of what, in my opinion, was an earnest desire on the part of the Department of Agriculture, including the minister, to do the best job they could for Canada, and I am not given to handing out bouquets where I do not feel they are deserved. I have presented many of our producer boards to the minister, and I would say that our producers, having come through a serious depression during the thirties, and having come into controlled position during the war, have submitted gracefully to the situation.

Agricultural Products Act
My good friend the hon. member for Middlesex West mentioned one of our commodities, beans. Some members of the house may smile when I mention beans. I could mention hybrid corn, onions-and this is not Mitchell Hepburn speaking-tobacco and other commodities. All these commodities mean a good deal to the economy not only of southwestern Ontario but of Canada as a whole. Were I to quote the excise revenue from tobacco alone, the house would be convinced of its importance to our economy. It is my opinion from what I have gleaned in the last few days-I have not the actual figures -that the revenue from tobacco alone was over $400 million.
As I said, my good friend from Middlesex mentioned beans. I place an entirely different interpretation on that situation. In 1940, the first year of the war, we found ourselves with a surplus of beans. We had a board but it had not been functioning actively up to that time. It had some difficulties in organization and in bringing together a majority of the producers of that commodity. We came to the department here in Ottawa and pleaded for a price that would relieve us of that surplus. We had no knowledge of how long the war would last or what it would mean in foodstuffs, and no knowledge of the tremendous drain we afterwards experienced on the young producers of our country.
Then we found ourselves running short of beans. Our primary producer group came to Ottawa and waited on the minister, on the special products board and the food board and asked for a price that would ensure a reasonable production of beans. After we had [DOT]entered into a contract with the British food ministry to provide Britain with a reasonable amount of beans in comparison with the lend-lease shipments of beans from the United States, our price was fixed at $2. That was not ample enough to bring about the desired production. In the year following, we entered into an arrangement and sold approximately one-third of our production to those who needed it so badly in the United Kingdom, but at a great sacrifice to the consumers of this country. We did not meet our quota but those beans were sold on the basis of $3 a bushel. Ours had been subsidized to the [DOT]extent of fifty cents. We were on the $2.50 level. We were operating on a participating [DOT]certificate in so far as our domestic market was concerned. That brought us up to $2.69 in *Canada as against $3' for our overseas commitments.
I would say to hon. members that when you .find a producer group vitally interested in the
perpetuation of an industry that is their bread and butter, that means their livelihood, medical attendance and education and everything else for their families, it means much more to them than it means to any minister of agriculture.

subtopic: PROVISION FOR PURCHASE, SALE AND EXPORT-COMMODITY AND PROVINCIAL MARKETING BOARDS
speechtext: That was done under the orders in council.

subtopic: PROVISION FOR PURCHASE, SALE AND EXPORT-COMMODITY AND PROVINCIAL MARKETING BOARDS
speechtext:
I thank the minister.
Take some of our other commodities; tobacco, for instance. We have fought and laboured to bring about a situation that would be satisfactory to our producer group. What have they accomplished? If we are to interfere with producer groups; if producer boards are to be shorn of the authority and powers they have exercised-I am not saying that governments should not play a part in it because we need their moral support and their assistance when it comes to disposing of an exportable surplus such as we may experience in the years that lie ahead-we do not want dictatorial powers given to any individual, whether it be a minister or someone else authorized to do that job. What we have done in our producer groups is this. We have convinced our processors, our distributors and our consumers that those who are most vitally interested in any business can handle it reasonably well.

subtopic: PROVISION FOR PURCHASE, SALE AND EXPORT-COMMODITY AND PROVINCIAL MARKETING BOARDS
speechtext: The government board has just as great powers as you asked for.

subtopic: PROVISION FOR PURCHASE, SALE AND EXPORT-COMMODITY AND PROVINCIAL MARKETING BOARDS
speechtext:
My interpretation of the bill may be wrong. I rose in rather an apologetic way because I had thought that when the federal agricultural marketing legislation was brought down I might even have to walk across the floor of the house, but I do not feel that I can do so now. I cannot see that it has provided for these groups what I hoped it might.
I listened attentively the other day to what was being said, and to show you, Mr. Speaker, how short my memory is, I have forgotten from whence it came, but I heard someone commending some hon. member in the house, or perhaps it was the minister, for the fact that the statistical branch in Ottawa was almost perfect. I disagree with that. All my experience with marketing organizations has been one with which I am in entire agreement. I have every respect for members of the government and the Department of Agriculture and the work they are attempting to do, but I feel they often get the cart before the horse.
One respect in which this is true is in connection with the duties assigned to our trade
Agricultural Products Act

commissioners. Trade commissioners may be selected on the basis of being bilingual, or the trade commissioner may be a Beau Brummel, one who is able to cope with social activities abroad, or it may be that he has an intimate knowledge of the commodity he is asked to dispose of and the markets which he is asked by the department to explore. But in all my experience with producer boards I have yet to see a trade commissioner come to us and ask for any guidance or direction. I am not saying that authority should be taken away from the government, but I feel that those who are vitally interested in their own affairs should not be discouraged by being shorn of that right. When jmu are part and parcel of an undertaking, that brings together the manufacturer, the distributor and the consumer; when you increase the price of the commodity substantially; when you maintain the dividends of the company and do not increase the cost to the consumer one iota, that is an accomplishment, and I would hesitate to go back to my producer groups if I felt I had not attempted to convince the minister; and I am doing so in a kindly way. At least, I hope I shall succeed, because I am vitally interested in this business of marketing, and I see no reason why the minister should take unto himself such authority and power. But if this is socialism in the mind of my hon. friend, then hon. members across the floor of the house who ordinarily cannot be classified as socialists, and who do not profess to be-and I refer to two of them in particular, namely the hon. member for Fort William (Mr. Mclvor), for whom I have a high regard, and the hon. member for Fraser Valley (Mr. Cruickshank) who contributes so delightfully to the debates of the house-both rise in their places and said that if this legislation is socialism, then they are socialists. In the face of this reconversion of political faith that is going on around us, I am afraid my hon. friends will be an island of resistance of their own.
