subtopic: PROVISION FOR PURCHASE, SALE AND EXPORT-COMMODITY AND PROVINCIAL MARKETING BOARDS
speechtext:
It is from Bracken's "Charter for a better Canada". There are a great many more delightful things in the pamphlet which I shall not take the trouble to quote. There is this, for example: compulsory collective bargaining and other things along that line. I am pointing that out only for this reason-and not because I want to have any quarrel with my hon. friends; I enjoy listening to them-that I believe there is too much of a tendency to try to create an ideological difference on a piece of legislation which had nothing to do with ideology, at all.
Marketing legislation is not primarily a political football to be kicked around. I hold in my hand a report the meeting held in this city recently by a number of representatives of agriculture, under the auspices of the Canadian Federation of Agriculture, which included practically all the chief farm organizations in Canada. I believe hon. members from all sides of the house were invited to attend, and a great many of them did. I was one of them. I felt that the farmers there represented farm organizations in every province. There were also representatives of the provincial governments of many of the provinces, and there was unanimous agreement that they wanted marketing legislation. They presented a draft bill, which the minister has in his possession.
Here are some of the reasons they wanted marketing legislation. I believe these point out definitely that what farmers are asking for is something which other organizations have already had for a period of time, and which the farmers find is working in the interests of those organizations, so that they want to copy it.
I would quote from what Mr. Hannam, president of the C.F.A. had to say on that occasion:
We have three-quarters of a million farmers in Canada. Working individually these farmers cannot have any plan for orderly marketing without rules to carry out the plan. Marketing legislation simply provides legal status for the rules agreed upon by the majority. Our producers have reasoned that if the great major-

Agricultural Products Act
ity agree on a marketing plan, then the will of the majority should prevail to carry out the plan.
So he goes on along that line, asking the government for marketing legislation. Another gentleman who spoke at that time was Mr. A.' K. Lloyd of British Columbia Tree Fruits Limited, who said:
Why is it necessary? In view of the complexity of modern agriculture, it is essential in order that the producer may obtain at the least expense the greatest possible proportion of the consumer dollar, that he accomplish his marketing in an orderly manner. Such legislation will enable him to avoid the uneconomical waste which too often has caused the difference between prosperity and failure.
It is quite clear that the farmers are becoming anxious and want to get the greatest possible portion of the consumer dollar for the products that they have to sell. In other words, they want to find the shortest direct route between the producer and the consumer. In doing that they want to utilize government machinery set up for that purpose. Mr. Lloyd goes on:
Without such legislation, the basic industry of the country and one which is absolutely essential to its welfare, is left to the mercies of anyone clever enough to exploit enough.
That is putting it pretty close to the line. When hon. members to my right get up and accuse us of wanting to institute some sort of socialism I would point out that here is a gentleman who is saying that all they want to do is to take the marketing of their product out of the hands of the people who may exploit them and put it in the hands of the people who are interested in the welfare of the producer. I wish to impress upon the minister that the gentlemen who attended that conference felt a sense of urgency in this matter. I think it is unfortunate that the minister has not given the assurance to the house for which we have asked, that legislation of this kind will be forthcoming early in the next session. It is quite apparent that we cannot get it during this session. I want to quote Mr. Lloyd to show the urgency that was felt in this matter. He said:
Already there is a noticeable drift from the farm to the city, and this is hardly to be wondered at when it is remembered that the average farmer will be working from sixty to seventy hours a week, whereas other unionized labour has already achieved a forty-four or forty-hour week. Action on the matter under discussion cannot be postponed without distastrous results.
That is placing it pretty squarely on the doorstep of the minister. It points out that, unless action is taken quickly, there will be disastrous results in the production end of things.
I should like to go on now to the resolution which was carried unanimously by that conference. May I again emphasize that the chairman of the conference invited members of parliament who attended, to present their views if they had any in opposition to the draft bill. He got up repeatedly and asked members who were opposed to a marketing act of that kind to state their views. In my hearing, at least not one member of any political group got up and expressed any views in opposition to it. The following resolution was passed unanimously:
That this conference convened by the Canadian Federation of Agriculture with representatives of major agricultural organizations in attendance from all sections of the dominion ask that the directors of the Canadian Federation of Agriculture convey to the dominion cabinet the unanimous request of this meeting that legislation in line with the attached draft of a farm products marketing act, be introduced at the present session of parliament.
They wanted it right away. It was in pursuance of that thought that we in this group tried to do the only thing we could do, move an amendment in order that this bill might be given further consideration in an appropriate committee where the views of these organizations could be heard. We would then have an opportunity of hammering out a marketing act which would be in line with what the farmers are asking for. We are not opposed to the principle of this bill. We are going to support the principle of the bill and we have moved an amendment in an attempt to give time, both to the minister and to the government as a whole and to the farm organizations to get together to formulate an appropriate marketing act.
The minister says that it cannot be done at this time on account of the time element, since his powers will expire at too early a date and he must have power to carry on. We are willing to take a reasonable stand. We are asking the minister again to give us the assurance that at the next session of the house he will bring down a marketing act in line with the proposals made by this organization. If we get that assurance we shall have something to go on and the organized farmers will have something to go on until next year,
I do not see how it will be possible for any hon. member to rise in his place and vote against a bill of this kind if he says that he believes in orderly marketing and in living up to the agreements that Canada has made for the supply of food to Britain. I respect the views of my hon. friends to my right when they get up and say that this is a private enterprise country and that therefore we must
Agricultural Products Act

' keep the government entirely out of business, let everyone run his own show. I respect their views, but the facts of the past and present do not bear out those views. It is no longer true to say that this is a private enterprise country. No one here can say it is entirely private enterprise. The events of modern times have brought us to the point where we must do cooperatively what we cannot do individually, and the marketing of farm products is one of those things.
Mr. JOHN T. HACKETT (Stanstead): Mr. Speaker, I wish to say a few words before the motion for second reading passes. I do not think the hon. member for Dauphin (Mr. Zaplitny) needs to be told that there is a great difference between the bill that is before us and the legislation which was passed in 1934. In 1934 boards were set up and powers were conferred upon the boards. We have transportation boards; we have all manner of organizations from courts down to temporary commissions and committees that are manned by appointees of the government. That is one of the accepted ways that democracy has of giving effect to the wishes of a democracy. I submit that that is an entirely different matter from the executive itself taking powers. In fact the difference is so pronounced that when war came we adopted this extraordinary method which the government seeks to perpetuate by this bill.
It is not my intention to rehearse the many arguments that have been put forward against the second reading of this bill, but there are one or two points I should like to accentuate. We have been told, not once but many times, that Canada has made agreements and that the agreements should be implemented. It does appear that Canada has made agreements, but because Canada has made agreements in an improper way it does not follow that we should indulge in further impropriety to give it execution. Agreements have been made under the W ar Measures Act after the war was over and when parliament was in session. Agreements have been made and are being made by _ the government when parliament is available to express its approval or otherwise of them, and I think it is pushing the argument a little far to say that because Canada has undertaken through, if you will, a usurpation of power to do certain things it behooves us to go farther and confer dictatorial powers on the government in order that they may be implemented.
This is not entirely a new device of government. You will recall, Mr. Speaker, that the provinces, for instance, did confer upon the federal cabinet the right to tax, but for a 
special purpose and for a definite time.
Nevertheless the government, in the exercise of those borrowed powers, used them not to win the war but to win an election. The government used the borrowing powers that it had got from the provinces to raise money to bring in something which, in itself, is good, the family allowance, but it nevertheless used the moneys that it had to win the war for the purpose of winning an election, and now it is using what it brought in by the improper use of these moneys, something that itself was good, as an argument to keep in perpetuity the taxing powers it borrowed for the duration of the war only. That kind of argument is not sound argument. That kind of argument is not one which appeals very much to my imagination or to any generous sentiments which I may have toward people who are in want.
If the government has made these agreements to sell wheat or bacon or other commodities, undoubtedly they must be carried out, but let them be carried out as the hon. member for Calgary West (Mr. Smith) has suggested, at the expense of the people as a whole and not by a few. These agreements should not be used to push the people into further subjugation. The minister says. "I need this bill in order that I may implement agreements which I have made; I must have these iron controls in order that I may carry out my agreement with Britain." That is not so.
May I go just one step farther and say that we have had evidence in the last few days of the great danger which arises from governments entering into negotiations and transactions which are beyond their proper sphere and scope. When a government enters into trade it then exposes the nation to all the bickering and dissatisfaction that arise out of trade and especially out of trade by people who are not skilled in trading. When a merchant in Canada sells something to a merchant in Britain or to a merchant in Italy and a dispute arises, they may submit their difference to the courts; but when a nation deals with a nation there is no arbitrament but that of war. In these days when we are talking so much about peace; when we are seeking an abiding peace we seem unnecessarily to be creating causes for dissension and disagreement by injecting nations into the buying and selling of commodities and into all the disputes and difficulties which arise out of the marketing of goods, and denying them at the same time the benefits of arbitration, of adjustment and of settlement or appeal to the courts. I submit that we have got ourselves into a frame of mind from which it is

Agricultural Products Act
becoming more and more difficult to escape. One has but to frequent any of the standing committees to hear deputy minister after deputy minister explaining to the committee that it is the policy of government that there be more control; that there be more government management; that there be greater interference by the administration in what up to now we have considered to be the private business of the people of Canada.
I submit to you again, Mr. Speaker, that what we need is not more controls, not more legislation hampering the natural activities and the business of the country, but a government with nerve enough to rid itself of the controls which are weighing upon us even now, although hostilities are over for well nigh two years.

I am very glad to be able to give my support again to the measure now before the house. I regret the confusion which seems to be unavoidable in regard to this legislation now before us.
